title: PowerInfer: Fast Large Language Model Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU
one_line: A GPU-CPU hybrid LLM inference engine that preloads statistically hot ReLU-family neurons into consumer-GPU VRAM and computes the input-dependent cold neurons on the CPU with AVX2, using online activation predictors, neuron-aware sparse operators, and an offline ILP placement policy.

repo.evidence: github.com/SJTU-IPADS/PowerInfer is the GitHub org of the authors' institute (paper byline: Institute of Parallel and Distributed Systems, SEIEE, Shanghai Jiao Tong University). The tree contains the actual system described in the paper, not a stub: GPU neuron-aware sparse kernels at ggml-cuda.cu:4479-4800, CPU AVX2 sparse kernels at ggml.c:13855-14760, the hybrid FFN graph at llama.cpp:4546-4757, and the SS6 ILP placement solver at powerinfer-py/powerinfer/solver.py. README.md:109 now points clones at github.com/Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer (the authors' successor org / commercial spin-out, README.md:13); same repository, MIT licensed, 9791 stars.
repo.badge_evidence: none found - searched the SOSP'24 ACM DL entry (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3694715.3695964) and the SJTU IPADS publication page; no ACM Artifacts Available/Evaluated/Reproduced badge surfaced, and the repo carries no badge image.

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official implementation under the authors' institute org, MIT licensed, containing the full system. Paper SS7 says the engine is llama.cpp + ~4200 lines of C++/CUDA; the corresponding code is present and readable: llama.cpp:4546-4757 (hybrid sparse FFN build), ggml-cuda.cu:4479-4800 + :8787-8801 (GPU neuron-aware operators and dispatch), ggml.c:13855-14760 (CPU sparse mul_mat/axpy with ggml_axpy_avx_f16 at :14292), llama.cpp:3082-3157 (neuron-placement loading), powerinfer-py/powerinfer/{solver.py,export_split.py} (SS6 offline solver and gpu_idx/gpu_bucket export). Not a placeholder, not binary-only, not plotting-scripts-only. Caveat noted but not disqualifying: the offline profiler (SS6.1 monitoring kernel) and the predictor-training code are NOT released (README.md:298 unchecked TODO); the published per-model activation_*.pt statistics substitute for the profiler on the 8 supported models.

H2_no_root.evidence: Documented build is a plain user-space CMake: 'cmake -S . -B build -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=ON' (README.md:117-122); CMakeLists.txt:252 requires CMake 3.17+ for the CUDA path (system cmake is 3.25.1) and CMakeLists.txt:254 uses find_package(CUDAToolkit), satisfied by the system nvcc 11.8. No kernel module, no eBPF, no perf_event, no KVM, no hugepage setup anywhere in the SOSP'24 tree. ggml.c:1906-1910 only opens /proc/sys/kernel/numa_balancing read-only to print a warning. The repo_facts 'sudo' hits are confined to .github/workflows/*.yml CI runners and .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.md; the .devops Dockerfiles are optional and their steps (CUDA base image + cmake build) are trivially replayable with conda/pip. The only runtime external call is system("python3 -m powerinfer ...") at llama.cpp:3134, which needs an activated conda env on PATH, not privilege. The multi-GPU/multi-node/CXL red flags in repo_facts all point into smallthinker/, an unrelated newer sub-project.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: The paper's own target is this machine class: PC-High in SS8.1 is an RTX 4090 24GB + 8-core CPU + PCIe 4.0; our RTX A5000 is also 24GB Ampere, so the VRAM constraint that the whole design is built around is identical. The CPU kernels require only AVX2 (README.md:81 'x86-64 CPUs with AVX2'; ggml_axpy_avx_f16 at ggml.c:14292), which the Threadripper 5955WX has - no AVX-512 is used - and we have 16 cores vs the paper's 8. Multi-GPU is an explicitly unimplemented TODO (README.md:300), so nothing assumes >1 GPU. Single machine throughout. Concern to note: 125 GiB host RAM vs the paper's 192 GiB means FP16 Falcon-40B (~87 GB resident) is tight and FP16 LLaMA2-70B (~150 GB) is out of reach; their INT4 forms (Fig. 13) fit easily, and the 7B/13B FP16 results (Table 4 row 1, Figs. 10/11) fit comfortably. Set -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86 since CMakeLists.txt:290-299 defaults to 52;61;70.

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: All dependencies are user-space installable: C++ side vendors ggml/httplib/json and needs only CUDA + pthreads; Python side is requirements.txt (numpy, sentencepiece, transformers, ./gguf-py, ./powerinfer-py) plus powerinfer-py/pyproject.toml:17-20 (torch>=2, cvxopt==1.3.2) - all pip/conda installable. Models, predictors AND the profiled activation statistics are public, ungated Hugging Face repos listed at README.md:145-186 (PowerInfer/ReluLLaMA-{7B,13B,70B}-PowerInfer-GGUF, PowerInfer/ReluFalcon-40B-PowerInfer-GGUF, PowerInfer/prosparse-llama-2-{7b,13b}-gguf, PowerInfer/Bamboo-*-gguf, originals under SparseLLM/*). Evaluation data is public: scripts/get-wikitext-2.sh for perplexity, and the paper's workloads are the public Alpaca and MohamedRashad/ChatGPT-prompts HF datasets (SS8.1). No proprietary traces anywhere. Gaps that do not trip the filter: no OPT PowerInfer weights are published (so Figs. 12/17/18 and the OPT rows of Table 8 are unreproducible even though build_opt() exists at llama.cpp:5086), and no predictor-training code, so new models cannot be sparsified.

reproduce.target: Table 4, row 'LLaMA(ReGLU)-13B-FP16': llama.cpp 49.91 ms/token -> PowerInfer 14.38 ms/token = 3.47x at 1.5K input / 256 output on PC-High. This supports the paper's central claim that neuron-granular GPU-CPU hybrid execution beats layer-granular offloading once the model exceeds VRAM - at the smallest model size where that claim is load-bearing (~26 GB FP16 weights + ~1.8 GB predictors does not fit in 24 GB, so the split is genuinely exercised).
reproduce.scale_down: Use PowerInfer/ReluLLaMA-13B-PowerInfer-GGUF (direct HF download, ~28 GB, ships the activation/ profiling stats) and PowerInfer/prosparse-llama-2-13b-gguf as a second point. RTX A5000 in place of the RTX 4090: absolute ms/token will be worse (~75% of the 4090's memory bandwidth, far less FP16 throughput) but the speedup ratio is the claim, and both arms use the same GPU; 16 Zen-3 cores vs 8 Raptor Lake cores is if anything favourable to the CPU half. Baseline: convert-dense.py -> dense FP16 GGUF -> stock llama.cpp at a late-2023 commit with -ngl tuned to fill 24 GB; if upstream rejects the dense GGUF (README.md:205 warns the activation function was altered), fall back to PowerInfer's own dense mode (-ngl, README.md:229-234) and state it - that is the same baseline the paper's +PO ablation uses. Prompts: 1.5K tokens sampled from Alpaca / ChatGPT-prompts, -n 256, -t 16. Avoid FP16 40B/70B entirely on this machine; use INT4 (Fig. 13) if a larger model is wanted.
reproduce.effort: 4-6 person-days + ~15-25 GPU-hours (dominated by ~60 GB of HF downloads, the dense-baseline conversion, and sweeping output lengths 8/128/512 across two models)
reproduce.rationale: Not H because there is no evaluation script for any paper figure - no eval/ directory, no plotting scripts, nothing that reproduces Figs. 10-18; the harness must be written on top of examples/main and examples/llama-bench. The llama.cpp baseline commit is unpinned and the dense-GGUF compatibility warning at README.md:205 is a genuine fork in the road. cvxopt==1.3.2 (powerinfer-py/pyproject.toml:19) is a hard 2023 pin whose cvxopt.glpk module solver.py:4 requires, and cp312 wheels are doubtful on a Python-3.12-default machine - a likely first-day blocker needing a 3.10/3.11 env. HEAD is 2026-05-11, ~18 months past publication, and now carries an unrelated second project under smallthinker/, so an older checkout may be needed. Not L because the build is a plain user-space CMake with no exotic deps, the exact Table 4 model is published as a ready-made GGUF bundling the profiling statistics, the ILP placement runs automatically on first load (llama.cpp:3088-3139), and the target number is a single ms/token value printed by examples/main.

addons.name: Calibrated placement solver: restore the communication constraint and replace frequency with impact
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that an ILP whose per-layer communication constraint C_l is calibrated from measured T_sync and per-neuron GPU/CPU times on the target machine, and whose objective weights neurons by contribution magnitude rather than raw activation frequency, improves decode tokens/s at a fixed VRAM budget compared with PowerInfer's shipped solver, on ReluLLaMA-13B (FP16) and Falcon(ReLU)-40B (INT4).
addons.mechanism: Three concrete changes. (i) The engine never passes --threshold when it invokes the solver (llama.cpp:3122-3133 builds the command line with only --activation/--layer/--neuron/--capacity/--vram-capacity/--output) and __main__.py:18 defaults it to 0, so solver.py's Constraint 2 degenerates to -sum(a) <= 0: Inequality 4 of SS6.3.1 is not actually enforced in the artifact. Add a micro-benchmark measuring T_sync (one intra-layer CPU->GPU merge) and per-neuron GPU/CPU compute time on this machine, derive C_l per layer, and thread it through. (ii) Replace v_i = f_i (Eq. 1, implemented as the raw activation counts loaded at solver.py:22) with v_i = f_i * E[|a_i|] * ||W_i||, profiled once per model by a ~100-line HF-transformers forward hook (the paper's profiler is unreleased but the hook is trivial for ReLU-family MLPs). (iii) Fix the VRAM accounting at llama.cpp:3117, which uses a magic 4.5 slice multiplier carrying the authors' own '// TODO: why 4.5, not 3?' comment and therefore mis-sizes neuron_cap.
addons.motivating_evidence: Fig. 15 attributes a jump from 7.80x to 11.69x on Falcon-40B purely to the ILP policy, but SS8.3.1 says the comparison point is a 'naive neuron partitioning policy that assigns neurons randomly to the GPU' - a weak baseline. Simultaneously the shipped solver disables the very communication constraint SS6.3.1 argues is essential (threshold defaults to 0 and is never passed), and the authors flag their own VRAM accounting as unexplained (llama.cpp:3117). Either outcome teaches something: if calibration helps, the paper under-delivers its own design on real hardware; if it does not, the '+Policy' contribution in Fig. 15 is mostly hot-first ordering rather than the ILP.
addons.feasibility_rationale: solver.py is 90 lines and export_split.py is 77; the T_sync micro-benchmark and the magnitude-profiling hook are each small standalone pieces. Total change is well under 1k LOC across two Python modules and one C++ call site. Evaluation reuses examples/main and examples/llama-bench on 13B FP16 and 40B INT4 models that fit this machine's 24 GB GPU and 125 GB RAM. Comfortably within 10 weeks for 2-4 students.
addons.research_value_rationale: It is a reproduction-grade correction plus a modest design improvement rather than a new mechanism. A SOSP reviewer would care that a headline ablation rests on a constraint the artifact does not enforce and on a deliberately weak baseline, but the achievable gain is bounded by how much neuron placement matters at all once the hot set is roughly right - so the upside is real but capped.

scoop_check.details: Queried 'PowerInfer neuron placement ILP solver reproduction communication constraint neuron impact metric improvement' and surveyed follow-up work citing PowerInfer. Nothing re-examines the fidelity of the released offline solver. The nearest adjacent work changes placement at runtime rather than fixing the offline formulation: DynamicInfer (ICLR 2026, https://openreview.net/forum?id=CvjmvjlczZ) and Q-Infer (ACM TACO 2025, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3764589). Neither touches C_l calibration or the impact metric.

addons.name: Co-allocate VRAM between hot neurons and the KV cache as a function of context length
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that dynamically splitting the VRAM budget between hot-neuron weights and KV-cache pages - instead of PowerInfer's fixed 'all VRAM to neurons, KV cache in host RAM' rule - reduces time-between-tokens by at least 15% at context lengths of 4K and above on a 24 GB GPU, while costing little or nothing at the 64-128 token contexts the paper evaluates.
addons.mechanism: SS7 states the KV cache 'continues to reside in CPU memory, allowing more GPU memory for hot-activated neurons', and the code only pulls K/V into VRAM in the degenerate case where every layer is already offloaded (llama.cpp:3399-3402 returns early unless n_gpu_layers >= n_layer+1). As context grows, per-token CPU attention work grows linearly while the marginal value of the n-th hot neuron falls off a power law (Fig. 4), so a crossover must exist. Add a KV term to the ILP: a second resource consumer with its own value function (measured CPU attention ms per 1K tokens of context) competing for the same MCap_GPU of Inequality 6, solved per n_ctx. On the engine side, extend llama_set_vram_budget / llama_reduce_vram_budget (llama.cpp:188-217) to reserve a context-dependent KV slice before llm_load_gpu_split runs, and let the KQV graph builder place K/V on whichever backend the policy chose. Evaluate a TBT-vs-context curve at 512 / 2K / 8K / 16K while sweeping the neuron:KV ratio.
addons.motivating_evidence: The KV-in-CPU decision is asserted in one sentence in SS7 with no sensitivity study, and the paper's longest input is 1.5K (Table 4). SS8.3.5 names the CPU as the entire remaining gap to the A100 ('The remaining disparity mainly stems from the CPU's considerable computational load, which has become a bottleneck'), and SS8.2 says the CPU becomes the primary bottleneck for long prompts. KV-cache attention is the one CPU cost that grows without bound in context length, unlike neuron compute which is capped by sparsity - so the paper's fixed rule is being validated only in the regime where it is cheapest to be right.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Cross-cutting: the ILP, the VRAM budgeting helpers, tensor backend assignment, and the attention graph all have to move together, and the KV-on-GPU path in this fork is only exercised in one degenerate configuration so it may need repair. A long-context prompt generator must be written. Compute is cheap (single-stream decode on a 13B model) and no new hardware is needed, but this is not a localized change.
addons.research_value_rationale: It attacks an unargued design assumption in precisely the regime the paper skips, and that regime - long chats, agent traces, RAG contexts - is the dominant local-deployment workload now. Either outcome is publishable-adjacent: a win shows the SOSP design leaves throughput on the table at realistic context lengths, and a clean negative ('KV in host RAM really is right even at 16K') establishes something the paper merely asserts.

scoop_check.details: Queried 'PowerInfer KV cache VRAM budget allocation tradeoff hot neurons long context CPU-GPU hybrid offloading' and 'joint allocation GPU memory between model weights and KV cache consumer GPU offloading'. Closest hits: HGCA: Hybrid GPU-CPU Attention for Long Context LLM Inference (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.03153), which optimizes the attention computation itself rather than trading KV against neuron weights under a single budget; and BaKlaVa (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.13176), which does per-head KV budget allocation in a dense GPU setting with no neuron offloading. Note also DynamicInfer (ICLR 2026, https://openreview.net/forum?id=CvjmvjlczZ), which re-partitions hot/cold neurons at runtime and reports 59% over PowerInfer - this scoops a naive 'make placement adaptive' idea, so this add-on is deliberately scoped to the neuron-vs-KV budget question, which DynamicInfer does not address.

addons.name: Activation-affinity request batching to preserve union sparsity at batch > 1
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that scheduling concurrent requests into batches by predicted neuron-set overlap - rather than by arrival order - raises end-to-end throughput by at least 20% at batch sizes 8-32 compared with PowerInfer's FIFO batching, because it keeps the union of activated neurons, and hence the total sparse work, small.
addons.mechanism: PowerInfer's batched sparse kernels take a per-row activation index and compute a row if any column in the batch wants it, so cost is the union of the batch's active sets (dequantize_mul_mat_batch_sparse, ggml-cuda.cu:4758-4800, gated by dev_sparse_threshold at :4786). Insert a scheduler in front of the server's batching loop that (i) runs the cheap predictor MLPs (llama.cpp:4688-4695) on each queued request's current hidden state, (ii) computes a signature (min-hash over the predicted-active neuron set), (iii) groups requests with high Jaccard similarity into the same micro-batch and runs dissimilar groups as separate micro-batches. Report tokens/s and p95 TBT versus batch size - a direct re-run of the Fig. 14 sweep with and without affinity grouping - plus measured union sparsity per batch as the mechanistic metric.
addons.motivating_evidence: Fig. 14 is the paper's own admission of the weakness: Falcon-40B speedup collapses from 11.69x at batch 1 to 4.38x at batch 32, which SS8.2 attributes to 'the diminished sparsity of model joint activations'. The paper treats this as a fact of life and never tries to schedule around it. SS3.1 / Fig. 5b supplies the mechanism that makes affinity grouping plausible: hot sets overlap >90% across task domains, so requests from similar domains should share neurons and requests from dissimilar domains should not be batched together.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The GPU and CPU kernels need no change - only the scheduling in front of them. But a new multi-request workload generator (arrival process, mixed task domains drawn from Alpaca/ChatGPT-prompts) and a scheduler inside examples/server/server.cpp are real work, and a predictor pre-pass has to be plumbed outside the normal graph execution. This is the 'needs a new evaluation harness' case; compute itself is modest and fits the machine.
addons.research_value_rationale: It reframes what the paper presents as a hardware/algebraic limitation as a scheduling problem, which is squarely a systems contribution a SOSP reviewer would engage with, and it targets the single axis on which PowerInfer visibly degrades. A negative result is also informative: it would show that per-token activation sets are far less clustered than Fig. 5b's aggregate, task-level statistics suggest.

scoop_check.details: Queried 'activation sparsity aware request batching union of activated neurons batch LLM inference offloading'. Polar Sparsity (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.14884) observes the identical union-sparsity collapse under batching but responds by shifting sparsity from MLP to attention heads on a single datacenter GPU - it does not schedule requests and has no CPU-GPU hybrid engine. Neuralink (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.19274) groups co-activated *neurons* as a weight-layout optimization on smartphones, not co-activating *requests*. The nearest threat is Q-Infer (ACM TACO 2025, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3764589), 'sparsity-aware dynamic scheduling' for GPU-CPU collaborative inference; the team should read it in week 1 and re-scope if it already performs request-level grouping.

addons.name: Sparsity-preserving chunked prefill instead of the dense-GPU fallback
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that chunked prefill with chunk size chosen so that per-chunk union activation sparsity stays above a target threshold - rather than PowerInfer's all-or-nothing switch to dense GPU computation - reduces time-to-first-token by at least 25% for prompts of 2K-8K tokens on a 24 GB GPU, for models whose dense weights do not fit in VRAM.
addons.mechanism: SS8.2 states that for long inputs 'PowerInfer switches to dense GPU computation during the prefill stage', which for a model larger than VRAM means streaming weights over PCIe - exactly the failure mode SS2.2 criticizes in FlexGen. Instead: split the prompt into chunks, run the predictors per chunk, and take the sparse hybrid path whenever the chunk's measured union sparsity exceeds a threshold, falling back to dense only for chunks that are effectively dense. The decision point is the full_gpu / gpu_offload_ratio branch in llm_build_ffn_sparse (llama.cpp:4672-4673) and the full_gpu fast paths in llm_build_sparse_mul_mat (llama.cpp:4570-4578) and llm_build_sparse_axpy (llama.cpp:4623-4631), which currently key off a static offload ratio rather than observed batch sparsity; the batched GPU sparse op is already available at ggml-cuda.cu:6994. Expose chunk size as a CLI flag alongside --vram-budget (common/common.cpp:566) and sweep it, reporting TTFT and per-chunk union sparsity.
addons.motivating_evidence: SS8.2: with long prompts and short outputs PowerInfer gains only 1.07x-4x, because 'each token activating a unique set of neurons, substantially diminishing activation sparsity. As a consequence, the CPU becomes the primary bottleneck'. Table 4 only probes the long-input case at 1.5K. Yet Fig. 14's batch-32 data point still shows 4.38x, direct evidence that meaningful sparsity survives at 32-wide token batches - which is exactly what a prefill chunk is. The binary dense/sparse switch is therefore leaving measurable headroom on the table in the regime the paper concedes is its weakest.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Localized in the graph builder (three call sites in llama.cpp) but it needs a runtime union-sparsity measurement feeding a per-chunk decision, and the batched sparse kernels must be exercised in a prefill regime they were not tuned for, so kernel-level surprises are likely. TTFT measurement is cheap and the whole study fits comfortably on one 24 GB GPU with a 13B model.
addons.research_value_rationale: Chunked prefill itself is standard practice elsewhere, so the mechanism is not novel; the novelty is the sparsity-driven chunk-sizing criterion and the fact that nobody has quantified the size of the dense-prefill cliff inside a hybrid offloading engine. A solid, somewhat expected improvement in a regime the paper explicitly sets aside - worth doing, unlikely to surprise a reviewer.

scoop_check.details: Queried 'sparse chunked prefill activation sparsity prompt phase PowerInfer hybrid CPU GPU TTFT'. Prefill-sparsity work exists but is token-selection on a dense GPU (SpecPrefill, ICML 2025, which keeps top-k% of prompt tokens by importance). SparseInfer (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.12692) predicts activation sparsity training-free for ReLU LLMs but does not address chunked prefill in a hybrid engine. DynamicInfer (https://openreview.net/forum?id=CvjmvjlczZ) includes an activation-aware prefetching pipeline that overlaps transfer with compute, which is adjacent but is about hiding transfer latency rather than sizing prefill chunks by union sparsity. Nothing found that sizes prefill chunks by measured union activation sparsity in a CPU-GPU offloading engine.

risks: Repo drift: HEAD is 2026-05-11, ~18 months after publication, and the tree now hosts an unrelated newer project (smallthinker/, a separate llama.cpp fork for 2025 SmallThinker MoE models with its own CMakeLists and submodules). A shallow clone cannot tell me whether the top-level SOSP'24 code still builds cleanly; the team should be ready to check out a late-2024 commit. Desk review cannot settle this.

cvxopt==1.3.2 is a hard 2023 pin (powerinfer-py/pyproject.toml:19) and solver.py:4 imports cvxopt.glpk, which only exists in GLPK-enabled builds. cp312 wheels are doubtful, and the machine's default Python is 3.12. Mitigation: a Python 3.10/3.11 conda env. If GLPK is unavailable entirely, solve_gpu_split must be ported to PuLP/HiGHS - about half a day, but a day-one surprise.

CMakeLists.txt:290-299 defaults CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES to 52;61;70, omitting sm_86. It should JIT from the compute_70 PTX on the A5000, but -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86 must be passed explicitly to avoid a slow or failing path.

Baseline ambiguity: README.md:205 warns that convert-dense.py output 'might not work properly with llama.cpp' because the activation function was altered for ReluLLaMA/ProSparse models. If upstream llama.cpp rejects the dense GGUF, the only remaining baseline is PowerInfer's own dense mode - defensible (it matches the paper's +PO ablation baseline) but weaker than the paper's stated comparison, and it must be disclosed.

Host-RAM ceiling: 125 GiB total, ~111 GiB free on a shared machine. FP16 Falcon-40B needs roughly 87 GB resident plus ~174 GB of disk for download-then-convert against ~257 GB free. Plan on INT4 for anything at or above 40B and do not attempt FP16 70B (~150 GB).

Unreproducible figures: no public OPT PowerInfer weights means Fig. 12 (neuron load breakdown), Fig. 17 (predictor overhead), Fig. 18 (the A100 comparison) and the OPT rows of Table 8 are unreachable, despite build_opt() existing at llama.cpp:5086. No A100 makes Fig. 18 unreachable regardless. The unreleased profiler and predictor-training code (README.md:298) mean the adaptive-predictor contribution of SS5.1 can be used but not re-derived.

The 'communication constraint is inert' finding underpinning add-on 1 is inferred from reading solver.py:52-59, __main__.py:18 and llama.cpp:3122-3133, not from execution. It should be confirmed by instrumenting the solver before A1's design is built on it.

A5000 is not a 4090: lower memory bandwidth and much lower FP16 throughput. Speedup ratios should hold since both arms use the same GPU, but absolute tokens/s will not match the paper, and the CPU-vs-transfer crossover of SS3.2 / Fig. 6 may shift - which is itself an argument for doing add-on 1's on-machine calibration.

Scoop pressure is real and rising: DynamicInfer (ICLR 2026) already does runtime hot/cold re-partitioning and reports 59% over PowerInfer, Q-Infer (TACO 2025) does sparsity-aware GPU-CPU dynamic scheduling, and Polar Sparsity, PowerInfer-2 and HGCA occupy adjacent ground. A naive 'make the placement adaptive' project is dead on arrival; week-1 reading of Q-Infer in particular should precede committing to add-on 3.
